newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - EMU wobbles but 1999 launch still likely.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - EMU wobbles but 1999 launch still likely.

text.p: Chances of European economic and monetary union (EMU) starting on time in 1999 have slipped to an average of 76 percent from 82 percent in May, a Reuters poll showed on Wednesday.

June's poll of 47 economists and political analysts across Europe was carried out between June 6 and 9 as France dithered over the ratification of a previously-agreed stability pact to enforce monetary discipline after the launch of the euro.

The result of the June poll, although down on May's figures, is a slight improvement from a poll conducted the day after the French election, when the average from 40 respondents put the likelihood at just 72 percent.

The surprise victory for Lionel Jospin's socialists in France last month and Germany's failed attempt to revalue gold reserves in a bid to boost government coffers has left the EMU timetable looking wobbly.
"I still firmly believe it will commence as scheduled but some political manoeuvring needs to be done before the situation will improve," said Juha Ahtola, chief economist at Merita Bank in Helsinki.
"But everyone believes the political grounds are so strong that EMU cannot burst into pieces because of this kind of situation," he added.
A delay was still seen as the least likely option with France and Germany maintaining their impetus behind EMU, the poll showed.
All 47 respondents said they saw a first wave made up of France and Germany, as well as Austria, Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.

"The political and economic costs (of failure) are just so great. The economic costs are an appreciation of the deutschemark and a possible recession in Germany which will certainly not help Chancellor Kohl's re-election chances in 1998," said Jim Fralick, director of European economics at Morgan Stanley in London.
The 46 respondents who gave percentage likelihoods for individual countries' membership put the average chances of the core six at 100 percent.

But the launch pad is set to encapsulate more than the top six, plus hot favourites Ireland and Finland, as it becomes clear that some tweaking of the Maastricht Treaty may be necessary, analysts said.

Spain and Portugal's chances of joining the single currency club in 1999 have soared. More than 70 percent thought the two Iberian countries would make the grade, compared to just 55 percent for Spain and 53 percent for Portugal in May's survey.
"The scales really tipped after the French election. The fact is there will be a much more flexible interpretation of the criteria," Fralick said.

Italy was also edging up in the stakes with 45 percent of respondents seeing it in the first wave versus 14 percent in May. In percentage likelihood terms, Italy looks to be in rather than out, with the median average at 60 percent compared to 40 percent last month.
If these countries are refused entry to the first wave, they are expected to join within 24 months of the start, the poll showed.
Sweden joined Britain and Greece at the rear after Prime Minister Goran Persson ruled out joining at the start in 1999.
Not one of the respondents thought that Sweden would be in the first wave and the median average delay predicted before it would join the currency club was 24 months.
